1. Core Clinical Tension: An adolescent female presents with severe biventricular dilated cardiomyopathy, upper extremity claudication, and peripheral lower limb pulse deficits accompanied by high systemic inflammatory markers and chronic constitutional wasting, where severe vascular-cardiac compromise overshadows an underlying granulomatous infectious etiology.
2. Admission Breakpoint: Outpatient evaluation and admission workup including history of exertional dyspnea and claudication, physical examination (axillary lymphadenopathy, absent lower extremity pulses, displaced PMI, murmur), baseline triage laboratories (anemia, lymphocytosis, elevated ESR/CRP), and bedside echocardiogram, stopping strictly before chest CT granuloma identification, aortic CT angiography, and lymph node fine needle aspiration biopsy.
3. Differential Distinctions: Primary dilated cardiomyopathy explains severe heart failure but fails to account for absent peripheral lower limb pulses, upper limb claudication, marked lymphadenopathy, and extreme inflammatory elevation. Primary systemic autoimmune arteritis (Takayasu) mimics large-vessel stenoses but requires distinguishing primary idiopathic autoimmune disease from infection-driven arteritis induced by chronic mycobacterial disease.
case_prompt:
A 14-year-old female from Ethiopia presents with worsening fatigue and resting shortness of breath of one week duration. Eight months prior to presentation, she developed progressive exertional dyspnea accompanied by two-pillow orthopnea and bilateral lower extremity swelling. Over the preceding year, she has noted difficulty combing her hair, intermittent claudication in her upper extremities during daily tasks, a chronic cough productive of whitish sputum, drenching night sweats, and marked unquantified weight loss. She denies headaches, visual disturbances, focal neurological weakness, chest pain, nausea, vomiting, cutaneous rashes, or photosensitivity ulcers. She has no prior personal or family history of chronic pulmonary illness or hypertension.

On physical examination, she appears chronically ill. A solitary, non-tender, firm lymph node measuring 2 x 3 cm is palpated in the left axillary fossa. Carotid, brachial, and radial pulses are symmetrically palpable with full volume and no audible bruits; however, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis pulses are absent bilaterally. Blood pressure measurements are 100/75 mmHg in the right arm, 105/68 mmHg in the left arm, 130/70 mmHg in the right popliteal artery, and 132/73 mmHg in the left popliteal artery. Cardiac examination reveals an active precordium, point of maximal impulse displaced to the sixth intercostal space, and a systolic murmur along the left sternal border. Abdominal examination is unremarkable.

Baseline laboratory studies demonstrate anemia with a normal total leukocyte count and predominant lymphocytosis. Inflammatory markers are elevated, with an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 100 mm/hr and a C-reactive protein of 14 mg/dL. Renal and liver function panels are within normal limits. Serologic testing for HIV and hepatitis C virus is non-reactive. Echocardiography shows dilated cardiomyopathy with biventricular systolic dysfunction (left ventricular ejection fraction approximately 15–20%), mild pulmonary hypertension, and moderate secondary mitral regurgitation.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to profound biventricular systolic dysfunction (LVEF 15–20%), secondary mitral regurgitation, and congestive heart failure symptoms, but primary myocardial disease does not account for peripheral pulse deficits, claudication, firm axillary lymphadenopathy, or an ESR of 100 mm/hr.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Echocardiography showed a dilated cardiomyopathy with biventricular systolic dysfunction (LV ejection fraction ~15-20%) with mild pulmonary hypertension and moderate secondary mitral regurgitation.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Isolated Systemic Autoimmune Vasculitis (Primary Takayasu Arteritis without Infection)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered given the large-vessel inflammatory stenoses, pulse discrepancies, and arm claudication in a young female, but the presence of caseating granulomatous lymphadenitis identified the arteritis as secondary to an underlying chronic infectious granulomatous process.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Computed angiography of the thoracic and abdominal aorta (Figures 1 and 2) showed diffuse and irregular narrowing of the distal descending thoracic and proximal abdominal aorta with partially thrombosed aneurysm of the proximal abdominal aorta... and the findings suggest Takayasu arteritis.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Fine needle aspiration of the enlarged left axillary lymph node demonstrated caseous necrosis and vague granulomas, with acid-fast bacilli confirmed on Ziehl-Neelsen staining, establishing tuberculous lymphadenitis as the primary inciting driver of active large-vessel arteritis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Fine needle aspiration of the enlarged lymph node showed mainly caseous necrosis and vague granuloma in a reactive lymphoid background. The specimen was stained with Ziehl-Neelsen, and acid-fast bacteria was detected confirming tuberculos lymphadenitis.

editor_comments: Case prompt isolates admission clinical and echocardiographic features before cross-sectional vascular imaging interpretations and lymph node biopsy histology. Zero pathogen disclosure in prompt. Exact verbatim quotes from article included.
